meta.title: MongoDB vs Redis (2026) - Which is better?

verdict: MongoDB is better for applications needing a flexible, persistent document database with rich queries and secondary indexes. Redis is better as an in-memory data store for caching, sessions, queues, and real-time low-latency workloads; in many architectures they complement rather than replace each other.

faq.a: Neither is universally better; they serve different purposes. MongoDB is a general-purpose document database with durable storage, ad hoc queries, aggregation, and transactions, making it suitable as a system of record. Redis is primarily an in-memory key-value store optimized for sub-millisecond latency, caching, and ephemeral data. Choose MongoDB for primary application data and Redis for caching, sessions, rate limiting, and real-time features.

Rarely as a full system of record. Redis offers persistence options (RDB snapshots, AOF logging) and modules, but its data model and memory-bound economics make it less suited to complex queries, large datasets, and flexible document storage. It can replace MongoDB only for simple, small, performance-critical datasets where durability and query flexibility are not primary concerns.

faq.q: Can MongoDB replace Redis for caching?
faq.a: Technically yes, but it is usually inefficient. MongoDB reads hit disk-backed storage and have higher latency than an in-memory cache, so using it as a cache layer increases load on the primary database. Redis is purpose-built for caching with TTLs, eviction policies, and in-memory speed.

faq.q: When should I use both MongoDB and Redis together?
faq.a: A common pattern is MongoDB as the source of truth for application data and Redis as a cache in front of it, plus for sessions, rate limiting, job queues, pub/sub, and leaderboards. This combination gives durable, queryable storage alongside low-latency access and real-time capabilities.

faq.q: Which is better for real-time applications?
faq.a: Redis is generally better for real-time features such as pub/sub messaging, presence, leaderboards, and caching because of its in-memory design and low latency. MongoDB supports change streams and can power reactive applications, but it is not optimized for high-frequency ephemeral operations the way Redis is.
